source_text: Primam igitur instrumentis istis auctoritatem summa antiquitas vindicat. Apud vos quoque religionis est instar, fidem de temporibus asserere. (Quae sequuntur uncis inclusa primus e cod. Fuldensi Havercampus publici juris fecit, sed alteri scriptoris recognitioni tribuens sub finem editionis suae experimenda curavit). [Primus enim prophetes Moyses, qui mundi conditionem et generis humani pullulationem et mox ultricem iniquitatis illius aevi vim cataclysmi de praeterito exorsus est, per vaticinationem usque ad suam aetatem et deinceps per res suas futurorum imagines edidit, penes quem et temporum ordo digestus ab initio supputationem saeculi praestitit: superior invenitur annis circiter trecentis, quam ille antiquissimus penes vos Danaus in Argo transvenisset; Trojano denique praelio ad mille annos ante est, unde et ipso Saturno. Secundum enim historiam Thalli, qua relatum est bellum Assyriorum et Saturnum Titanorum regem cum Jove dimicasse, ostenditur bellum CCCXX. et duobus annis Iliacum exitium antecessisse. Per hunc Moysen etiam illa lex propria Judaeis a Deo missa est. Deinceps multa et alii prophetae vetustiores litteris vestris. Nam et qui ultimo cecinit, aut aliquantulo praecucurrit, aut certe concurrit aetate sapientiae auctoribus, etiam latoribus legis. Cyri enim et Darii regno fuit Zacharias, quo in tempore Thales physicorum princeps, sciscitanti Croeso nihil certum de Divinitate respondit, turbatus scilicet vocibus prophetarum, Solon eidem regi finem longae vitae intuendum praedicavit non aliter, quam Prophetae; adeo respici potest, tam jura vestra quam studia de lege deque divina doctrina concepisse. Quod prius est, hoc sit semen necesse est. Inde quaedam nobiscum vel prope nos habetis. De sophia amor ejus philosophia vocitatus est, de prophetia affectatio ejus poeticam vaticinationem depuravit. Gloriae homines, si quid invenerant, ut proprium facerent, adulteraverunt; etiam fructibus a semine degenerare contigit. Multis adhuc de vetustate modis consisterem divinarum litterarum, si non major auctoritas illis ad fidem de veritatis suae viribus, quam aetatis annalibus suppetisset. Quid enim potentius patrocinabitur testimonio earum, nisi dispunctio quotidiana saeculi totius, cum dispositiones regnorum, cum casus urbium, cum exitus gentium, cum status temporum ita omnibus respondent, quemadmodum ante millia annorum praenuntiabantur? Unde et spes nostra, quam ridetis, animatur, et fiducia, quam praesumptionem vocatis, corroboratur. Idonea est enim recognitio praeteritorum ad disponendam fiduciam futurorum: eadem voces praedicaverunt utramque partem, eadem litterae notaverunt. Unum est tempus apud illas, quod apud nos separari videtur. Ita omnia quae supersunt improbata sunt nobis, quia cum illis, quae probata sunt, tunc futuris praedicabantur. Habetis, quod sciam, et vos Sibyllam, quatenus appellatione ita vera vates dei veri passim super caeteros, qui vaticinari videbantur, usurpata est, sicut vestrae Sibyllae nomen de veritate mentitae, quemadmodum et dei vestri.] Omnes itaque substantias, omnesque materias, origines, ordines, venas veterani cujusque styli vestri, gentes etiam plerasque et urbes insignes, historiarum canas, et memoriarum, ipsas denique effigies litterarum, indices custodesque rerum, et (puto adhuc minus dicimus) ipsos inquam deos vestros, ipsa templa et oracula et sacra unius interim prophetae scrinium saeculis vincit, in quo videtur thesaurus collocatus totius Judaici sacramenti, et inde etiam nostri. Si quem audistis interim Moysen, Argivo Inacho pariter aetate est; quadringentis pene annis, nam et septem minus, Danaum, et ipsum apud vos vetustissimum, praevenit, mille circiter cladem Priami antecedit; possem etiam dicere, quingentis amplius et Homerum, habens quos sequar. Caeteri quoque prophetae, etsi Moysi posthumant, extremissimi tamen eorum non retrosiores deprehenduntur primoribus vestris sapientibus et legiferis et historicis. Haec quibus ordinibus probari possint, non tam difficile est nobis exponere, quam enorme, nec arduum, sed interim longum. Multis instrumentis, cum digitorum supputariis gesticulis assidendum est. Reseranda antiquissimarum etiam gentium archiva, Aegyptiorum, Chaldaeorum, Phoenicum; advocandi etiam municipes eorum, per quos notitia subministrata est; aliqui Manethon Aegyptius, et Berosus Chaldaeus, sed et Iromus Phoenix Tyri rex; sectatores quoque eorum Mendesius Ptolemaeus, et Menander Ephesius, et Demetrius Phalereus, et rex Juba, et Appion, et Thallus, et qui istos aut probat aut revincit, judaeus Josephus antiquitatum Judaicarum vernaculus vindex. Graecorum etiam censuales conferendi, et quae quando sint gesta, ut concatenationes temporum aperiantur, per quae luceant annalium numeri. Peregrinandum est in historias et litteras orbis. Et tamen quasi partem jam probationis intulimus, quum per quae probari possint, aspersimus. Verum differre praestat, ne vel minus persequamur festinando, vel diutius evagemur persequendo.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the highest antiquity claims the first authority for these instruments. Also among you, it is a model of religion to assert faith from times. For Moses, the first prophet, who began from the past to recount the condition of the world and the multitude of the human race and soon the avenging force of the wickedness of that age through the flood, produced images of future things through prophecy up to his own time and thereafter through his own deeds. He also arranged the order of times from the beginning, providing a calculation of the age, which is found to be about three hundred years earlier than Danaus, who came to Argos in the Argo. Moreover, the Trojan war is about a thousand years before, from which also Saturn. For according to the history of Thallus, which reports the war of the Assyrians and Saturn, the king of the Titans, fighting with Jupiter, it is shown that the war preceded the destruction of Ilium by three hundred and two years. Through Moses, the law proper to the Jews was also sent by God. Afterwards, many other prophets, older than your writings, followed. For even the one who sang last, or ran ahead by a little, or certainly coincided in age with the authors of wisdom and also the bearers of the law, was Zacharias, who was in the reign of Cyrus and Darius, at which time Thales, the prince of physicists, responded to Croesus, who was inquiring, that nothing certain could be said about Divinity, clearly disturbed by the voices of the prophets. Solon also predicted to the same king the end of a long life, not otherwise than the prophets. So it can be seen that both your laws and studies have conceived from the law and divine doctrine. What is prior must necessarily be the seed. From this, you have certain things with us or near us. The love of wisdom has been called philosophy, and the affectation of prophecy has purified poetic prophecy. Famous men, if they found something, adulterated it to make it their own, and it also happened that the fruits degenerated from the seed. I would still insist on many modes of the antiquity of divine writings, if a greater authority for faith in their truth did not suffice than the annals of years. For what is more powerful than the daily testimony of the whole age, when the dispositions of kingdoms, the falls of cities, the exits of nations, and the states of times respond to all, just as they were predicted thousands of years before? From this, our hope, which you ridicule, is encouraged, and the confidence, which you call presumption, is strengthened. The recognition of past things is indeed suitable for arranging confidence in future things: the same voices predicted both parts, the same writings noted them. There is one time among them, which seems to be separate among us. So all the things that remain are disapproved by us, because they were predicted as future things along with those that were approved. You also have, as far as I know, the Sibyl, insofar as the name of the true prophet of the true God has been usurped passim over the others, who seemed to prophesy, just as the name of your Sibyl is a lie from the truth, as also your gods. Therefore, all substances, and all materials, origins, orders, and veins of every old style, and most nations and notable cities, the white hairs of histories and memories, and finally the very images of writings, the indices and guardians of things, and (I think we say less) even your gods, their temples and oracles and sacred rites, are surpassed by the repository of one prophet, Moses, which contains the treasure of the whole Jewish sacrament, and from it also ours. If you have heard of Moses, he is of the same age as Argive Inachus; he precedes Danaus by almost four hundred years, and the destruction of Priam by about a thousand years; I could also say that he precedes Homer by more than five hundred years, having those whom I can follow. The other prophets, although they are later than Moses, are nevertheless not found to be more recent than your first wise men and lawgivers and historians. It is not so difficult for us to explain the orders by which these things can be proven, as it is enormous, nor is it hard, but rather long. Many instruments must be used, with gestures of fingers and calculations. The archives of the most ancient nations, the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Phoenicians, must be opened; their citizens must also be summoned, through whom knowledge has been provided; some, such as Manetho the Egyptian, and Berosus the Chaldaean, but also Iromus, the Phoenician king of Tyre; and also the followers of these, Mendesius Ptolemaeus, and Menander of Ephesus, and Demetrius of Phalera, and King Juba, and Appion, and Thallus, and the Jew Josephus, the native defender of Jewish antiquities, who either approves or refutes them. The censuses of the Greeks must also be compared, and the times when things were done, so that the concatenations of times may be revealed, through which the numbers of annals may be clarified. One must wander through the histories and writings of the world. And yet, we have already introduced a part of the proof, when we sprinkle the things by which they can be proven.

pass_b_english: The highest antiquity claims the first authority for these writings. Among you, too, asserting faith from the records of time is a kind of religious standard.

Consider Moses, the first prophet. He began with the creation of the world, the multiplication of the human race, and the avenging force of the flood that punished the wickedness of that age. Through prophecy he sketched images of future events up to his own day, and through his own actions thereafter. He also arranged the chronological order from the beginning, providing a calculation of the world's age that predates your earliest records by about three hundred years — earlier than Danaus who sailed to Argos in the Argo, and roughly a thousand years before the Trojan War, from which you even trace Saturn himself. Thallus' history corroborates this: it records the war of the Assyrians and the battle of Saturn, king of the Titans, against Jupiter, showing that this war preceded the fall of Ilium by 302 years. Through Moses, God also gave the Law proper to the Jews.

After him came many other prophets, older than your literature. Even the last of them, Zechariah — who either slightly anticipated or at least coincided with your sages and lawgivers — prophesied under Cyrus and Darius. In that era, Thales, the prince of physicists, could give Croesus no certain answer about the Divine, clearly unsettled by the prophets' voices. Solon likewise warned that same king to look to the end of a long life, in terms no different from the prophets'. Thus it is evident that both your laws and your philosophical studies have drawn their conception from the Law and divine teaching. What comes first must be the seed; from it you hold certain things in common with us, or at least near us. The love of wisdom was named philosophy; the emulation of prophecy refined poetic prophecy into something purer. Famous men, when they discovered something, adulterated it to claim it as their own, and the fruits degenerated from the seed. I could press many more arguments for the antiquity of the divine writings, but a greater authority supports faith in their truth than mere annals: the daily testimony of the whole age. The dispositions of kingdoms, the falls of cities, the exits of nations, the conditions of the times — all answer to what was predicted thousands of years ago. From this our hope — which you mock — is encouraged, and our confidence — which you call presumption — is strengthened. Knowledge of the past is the proper basis for confidence in the future: the same voices foretold both, the same writings recorded them. There is a single timeline in Scripture that appears divided to us. Therefore we reject everything that remains unfulfilled, because those things were predicted as future alongside the ones already verified.

You also possess, as far as I know, the Sibyl — insofar as the title of the true prophet of the true God has been usurped by her above all others who seemed to prophesy, just as your Sibyl's name is a lie from the truth, and so are your gods. Therefore the archive of a single prophet — Moses — surpasses all substances, all materials, origins, orders, and veins of every ancient style of yours, most nations and notable cities, the hoary records of histories and memories, the very images of writings, the indices and guardians of facts, and (I think we understate it) even your gods themselves, their temples, oracles, and sacred rites. In that archive lies the treasure of the entire Jewish sacrament, and from it, ours as well. If you have heard of Moses, know that he is coeval with Argive Inachus; he precedes Danaus by nearly four hundred years — seven years short — and the fall of Priam by about a thousand. I could even say he predates Homer by more than five hundred years, and I have authorities to follow. The other prophets, though later than Moses, are still not more recent than your earliest sages, lawgivers, and historians. Demonstrating the chronological orders that prove this is not so much difficult as enormous — not arduous, but long. It requires many instruments, with finger-reckoning and calculations. The archives of the most ancient nations — Egyptians, Chaldeans, Phoenicians — must be opened; their own citizens must be summoned, through whom knowledge was transmitted: Manetho the Egyptian, Berosus the Chaldean, and Iromus the Phoenician king of Tyre; also their followers — Ptolemy Mendesius, Menander of Ephesus, Demetrius of Phalerum, King Juba, Apion, Thallus, and the Jew Josephus, native defender of Jewish antiquities, who either confirms or refutes them. Greek censuses must be compared, and the dates of events correlated, so that the concatenations of time are revealed and the numbers of annals clarified. One must traverse the histories and writings of the world. And yet we have already introduced a portion of the proof, by merely touching on the means by which it can be proven. But it is better to defer the rest, lest in haste we pursue it insufficiently, or in thoroughness we wander too long.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and the polemical tone of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, high-quality English version that preserves all nuances, including the specific years (302, 400, 1000, 500) and the list of historical authorities. All scripture-alluded content (Moses, Zacharias, etc.) is handled correctly.
